propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of RPD decision refusing refugee claim and finding viable IFA in Medellín, Colombia.
propositions.quote: The Applicants, Maribel Del Rosario Osorio Visbal (the “Principal Applicant”) and her minor son, Gabriel Andres Acuna Osorio (together as the “Applicants”) seek judicial review of a decision by the Refugee Protection Division (“RPD”), refusing their claim for refugee protection, finding a viable Internal Flight Alternative (“IFA”) in Medellín, Columbia.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants seek judicial review of RPD decision refusing refugee claim and finding viable IFA in Medellín, Colombia, court states.

propositions.text: Granting extension of time for Applicants to file application as conditions met and Respondent consents.
propositions.quote: I am granting an extension of time for the Applicants to file their application as the conditions are met and the Respondent consents (Canada (AG) v Henneley, (1999) 244 NR 399 (FCA)).

paragraphs.summary: Court grants extension of time for Applicants to file application as conditions met and Respondent consents.

propositions.text: Applicants allege well-founded fear of persecution due to political opinion, specifically opposition to ELN.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are citizens of Colombia, and allege that they have a well-founded fear of persecution because of their political opinion, specifically, their imputed opposition to the National Liberation Army or Ejército de Liberación Nacional (“ELN”).

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege well-founded fear of persecution due to political opinion, specifically opposition to ELN.

propositions.text: RPD found Principal Applicant generally credible but embellishing danger inferences beyond evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD Member found that the Principal Applicant was generally credible, but that her inferences regarding the danger she and her son would be in “went beyond what the evidence would support” and that she was embellishing her case in that respect.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Principal Applicant generally credible but embellishing danger inferences beyond evidence.

propositions.text: ELN demanded farm land owned by Principal Applicant’s ex-husband and siblings who refused.
propositions.quote: The Applicants claim that the ELN had demanded the farm land owned by the Principal Applicant’s ex-husband and his siblings, who refused to let them use or have it.

propositions.text: In Feb 2018, armed men approached Applicants, took son, wanted to recruit him into ELN, took money, said they wanted farm.
propositions.quote: In February 2018, the Applicants were approached by armed men. The Principal Applicant say the men took hold of her son, and said they wanted to recruit him into the ELN. Ultimately, they took money and the men stated that what they really wanted was the farm.

propositions.text: In May 2018 in Bogotá, son threatened with knife by man asking about marijuana and address.
propositions.quote: In May 2018, after the Applicants moved to Bogotá, the Principal Applicant’s son was walking through a campground when a man approached him and asked him for an address and whether he had marijuana in his backpack. When her son said he had no marijuana he threatened him with a knife.

propositions.text: Assailants told son he would not escape and to tell parents; family left Bogotá but returned in June 2018.
propositions.quote: The assailants told the son “even if you are in, you will not escape from us tell your parents.” (CTR pg 89) They left Bogata but returned in June 2018.

propositions.text: Son recognized man who threatened him in Bogotá; family returned to Barranquilla in July 2018 and complied with Attorney General summons.
propositions.quote: In Bogota the son recognized the man who had threatened him and sought an address and marijuana so the family returned to Barranquilla in July, 2018. They returned as well to comply with a summons from the Attorney General’s Office.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants say ELN demanded farm land; armed men threatened son in Bogotá; family left and returned to Barranquilla and complied with summons.

propositions.text: Ex-husband made denunciation to Attorney General, received ELN threat pamphlets declaring them military targets.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant’s ex-husband made a denunciation at the Attorney General Office, which amplified her previous denunciation. He had also been receiving “pamphlets” from the ELN with threats, and wherein the ex-husband and the Principal Applicant were declared “military targets.”

propositions.text: Ex-husband involved in shooting attempt by unknown man on motorcycle; Principal Applicant made denunciation on Aug 21, 2018.
propositions.quote: Her ex-husband was involved in a shooting attempt by an unrecognized man on a motorcycle of which he was not shot. She made a denunciation on August 21, 2018 to the Attorney General about this incident.

paragraphs.summary: Ex-husband made denunciation, received ELN threat pamphlets declaring them military targets, and survived shooting attempt; Principal Applicant made denunciation.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant treated for mitral regurgitation and mental health challenges in Colombia.
propositions.quote: Throughout her time in Colombia, the Principal Applicant was treated for a mitral regurgitation and mental health challenges.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant treated for mitral regurgitation and mental health challenges in Colombia.

propositions.text: Applicants flew to Buffalo in Aug 2018 but did not claim asylum; crossed into Canada and claimed asylum due to family there.
propositions.quote: After receiving advice from an official at the Office of the Attorney General, the Applicants flew to Buffalo, New York in August 2018, but did not make asylum claims, as they had no relatives in the USA. They then crossed into Canada and made an asylum claim, given that they had family in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants flew to Buffalo in Aug 2018 but did not claim asylum; crossed into Canada and claimed asylum due to family there.

propositions.text: In Canada, Principal Applicant’s sister was struck by men on motorcycle who mentioned Principal Applicant by name, believed ELN.
propositions.quote: Since being in Canada, the Principal Applicant’s sister was struck by two men on a motorcycle, who then mentioned the Principal Applicant by name. She believes that they were from the ELN.

paragraphs.summary: In Canada, Principal Applicant’s sister was struck by men on motorcycle who mentioned Principal Applicant by name, believed ELN.

propositions.text: Issue is whether RPD’s finding that Medellín is a viable IFA is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The issue is whether there the finding from the RPD that Medellín would be a viable IFA is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Issue is whether RPD’s finding that Medellín is a viable IFA is reasonable, court states.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness (Canada v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65).
propositions.quote: The standard of review is one of reasonableness (Canada v Vavilov (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 SCC 65).

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review is reasonableness, court states citing Canada v Vavilov.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant argues RPD erred by incorporating credibility findings into IFA analysis and ignoring evidence under both IFA prongs.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant submits that in finding that there was a viable IFA, the RPD erred by incorporating credibility findings into its IFA analysis, and that the RPD ignored and misconstrued the evidence under both prongs of the IFA test.

propositions.text: RPD accepted details of threats but unreasonably concluded ELN would not track them in other cities.
propositions.quote: She says that the RPD accepted all the details regarding their movements and having been targets throughout Colombia, including the threats in Bogotá and near her ex-husband’s family owned farm. She says, however, that the RPD’s conclusion that the ELN would not have the means or motive to track them in other cities is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Cites Aigbe v Canada to support argument that RPD’s conclusion is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In support of her submissions, she cites Aigbe v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 895 [Aigbe].

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant argues RPD erred by incorporating credibility findings into IFA analysis, ignoring evidence, and cites Aigbe v Canada.

propositions.text: In Aigbe, RAD assumed credibility but unreasonably inferred agent unlikely to find applicants if not living with family.
propositions.quote: In Aigbe, the Court ruled that having assumed that the applicants were credible, the Refugee Appeal Division (“RAD”)’s first prong analysis of the IFA test was based on an inference that the agent of persecution would be unlikely to find the applicants as long as they were not living with family.

propositions.text: Instant case similar; RPD failed to explain how evidence supports conclusion ELN would not track them after Bogotá incident.
propositions.quote: She asserts that the instant case is similar. She states the decision is unreasonable, given that the RPD failed to explain how the evidence supported the conclusion that they would not be tracked down by the ELN, after they had managed to do so in Bogotá.

propositions.text: Cites Ng’aya that IFA location eventually known renders it unsuitable.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant submits, citing Ng’aya v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1136 [Ng’aya], that when an IFA location would eventually become known it is rendered, unsuitable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Aigbe supports that RPD’s IFA finding is unreasonable and cites Ng’aya on IFA location becoming known.

propositions.text: Ng’aya means IFA is unreasonable if applicant must isolate totally from family and acquaintances, an impossible burden.
propositions.quote: In my view, it stands for the proposition that where an applicant’s whereabouts would eventually become known in the event they are unable or unwilling to isolate themselves totally from all of the other members of their family and past family acquaintances. This type of isolation is an impossible burden to place upon someone given the applicant in that case is personal circumstances (she was a young woman looking after a baby in a challenging and unfamiliar urban setting).

propositions.text: This case is not one where total isolation is required; Ng’aya does not apply here.
propositions.quote: I do not find that this is such a case.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Ng’aya means total isolation is impossible burden; this case does not require such isolation.

propositions.text: ELN knowing they fled Colombia shows sufficient info; RPD ignored this evidence.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant also says that because the ELN knew they fled Colombia, it demonstrates that they had sufficient information about them, and that the RPD ignored this (and other) evidence.

propositions.text: RPD accepted ELN can track individuals but rejected possibility they would track Applicants, unsupported by evidence.
propositions.quote: Further, she says that given the RPD accepted that the ELN can track individuals down, their rejection of the possibility that they would track down the Applicants is unsupported by the evidence.

propositions.text: Evidence shows military targets are targeted by ELN; cites AB v Canada that lack of motive or means is unreasonable when evidence shows repeated visits.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant points to evidence in the record which supports that military targets are targeted by the ELN. She cites Justice Manson in AB v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 915, for the principle that it is unreasonable for a decision-maker to justify a lack of motivation or means when the evidence shows consistent repeated visits.

propositions.text: RPD had duty to address contradictory evidence; failure renders decision unreasonable (citing Yahia).
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant suggests that the RPD Member had a duty to address the evidence which contradicted its conclusions (Yahia v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 84 at para 45), and that a failure to do so renders the decision unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues ELN knew they fled, RPD ignored evidence, and failed to address contradictory evidence, citing AB and Yahia cases.

propositions.text: RPD characterized health issues as stress-related; Applicant diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety, making finding unreasonable.
propositions.quote: On the second prong, she argues that the RPD characterized her health issues only as “stress-related,” and that she had been diagnosed with Post-traumatic Stress Disorder (“PTSD”) and Severe Generalized Anxiety Disorder, in addition to physical health problems. The Principal Applicant’s position is that this renders the finding unreasonable,

propositions.text: Psychological evidence central to IFA reasonableness and cannot be disregarded (citing Cartagena).
propositions.quote: citing case law which states that “psychological evidence is central to the question of whether the IFA is reasonable and cannot be disregarded” (Cartagena v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 289 at para 11).

propositions.text: Healthcare dependent on employment; returning to Colombia would worsen health.
propositions.quote: She also argues that her healthcare is dependent on employment, and that if she were to return to Colombia, her health would get worse.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD wrongly minimized health issues, citing PTSD diagnosis and psychological evidence importance, and worsening health if returned.

propositions.text: IFA two-pronged test: secure circumstances ensuring basic rights; and unreasonableness of seeking refuge there.
propositions.quote: In Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1991] FCJ No 1256, [1992] 1 FC 706, the well-established two-pronged test for an IFA is set out, requiring that: First, the Board must be satisfied on the evidence before it that the circumstances in the part of the country to which the claimant could have fled are sufficiently secure to ensure that the appellant would be able "to enjoy the basic and fundamental human rights". Second, conditions in that part of the country must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Rasaratnam two-pronged IFA test: secure circumstances and unreasonableness of seeking refuge there.

propositions.text: RPD found Medellín large city, Applicants not primary targets, no evidence ELN has means or motive to find them, so unlikely to be found.
propositions.quote: In their decision, the RPD stated that because Medellín is a large city and the Applicants are not primary targets, along with the fact that there is no evidence that the ELN has the means or motivation to find them. Given this, the RPD found that it was unlikely they would be found there.

propositions.text: Onus on Applicants to show proposed IFA unacceptable (Argote; Figueroa).
propositions.quote: It is true that the onus is on the Applicants to show that the proposed IFA would be unacceptable (Argote v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 128 at para 12; Figueroa v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 521).

propositions.text: Court finds RPD reasonable in determining Medellín is viable IFA given size, Applicants not primary targets, and no evidence of targeted search.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD was reasonable in their determination that, given Medellín is a large city, the Applicants are not primary targets, and the fact that she was not married to the target. The RPD Member says: “I have no idea how the minor claimant was located by the ELN in Bogotá, and neither do the claimants.” As a result, though the reasons do not extensively explain why Medellín would be different than Bogata other than it is a larger city, there is no evidence adduced that this was anything more than a random sighting by the son, and there was no evidence that he was being searched for by the individual he saw.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Medellín viable IFA as large city, Applicants not primary targets, no ELN search evidence; court finds this reasonable.

propositions.text: RPD found ELN looking for ex-husband over land, Applicants only second-hand military targets, ELN’s ability to track scarce.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s further supported their finding, when they considered the motive of the ELN to find the Applicants, that “I do not accept this response because I find that the claimants have not demonstrated that the ELN has the motive or the means to have instituted an ongoing, country-wide search for the claimants” (RPD Decision, para 36). As well, the RPD found that the ELN was looking for her ex-husband because he did not transfer land to them. It was him they were after. Further, the RPD stated that the Applicants had only heard second-hand that they were also military targets because of the farmland refusal, and there is no evidence of what the ELN wanted the land for (RPD Decision, para 37). This, taken in tandem with the country condition information and the ELN’s highly decentralized organizational structure, indicates that the ELN’s “…ability to track people is scarce” (RPD Decision, para 38).

propositions.text: RPD used objective evidence and Applicants’ evidence to reasonably find Medellín was an IFA meeting Vavilov reasonableness criteria.
propositions.quote: The RPD used this objective evidence, in light of the Applicants evidence – including the threats, as well as the uncertainty as to how the son was located in Bogota – and found reasonably that Medellín was an IFA. These factors, taken together, satisfy me that the criteria for reasonableness as set out in Vavilov are met on this prong of the 2-pronged test.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found ELN sought ex-husband, Applicants only second-hand targets, ELN’s tracking scarce; court finds RPD’s Medellín IFA finding reasonable.

propositions.text: RPD found it not unreasonable for Applicants to relocate to Medellín; Principal Applicant could earn living and health issues not hindering resettlement.
propositions.quote: Regarding the second prong of the test, the RPD explained why they found that it would not be unreasonable for the Applicants to relocate in Medellín. Based on the evidence of the Principal Applicant’s experience, the RPD concluded that she could earn a living and support herself. The RPD accepted the health issues of the Principal Applicant, but were unable to see how they would hinder her resettlement.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD’s reasons sufficient, internally coherent, rational, justified, and defers under reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: In my opinion, these reasons are sufficient. As required by Vavilov at paragraph 85, they are based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker. The reasonableness standard requires that a reviewing court defer to such a decision.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found relocation to Medellín not unreasonable; court finds reasons sufficient, coherent, justified, and defers under reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Neither party submitted a certified question and none arose from the application
propositions.quote: Neither party submitted a certified question and none arose from the application

propositions.text: Extension of time on consent of Respondent is granted for filing the Application
propositions.quote: The extension of time on consent of the Respondent is granted for the filing of the Application

propositions.text: The application is dismissed
propositions.quote: The application is dismissed

propositions.text: No question is certified
propositions.quote: No question is certified

paragraphs.summary: The court states no certified question was submitted or arose, grants extension of time on consent, dismisses the application, and certifies no question.
